concepts.def: 1818 sonnet; ruined statue inscribed 'Look on my Works'; mocks tyrants; nothing remains; sands stretch around.
1794 Songs of Experience; 'marks of weakness, marks of woe'; 'mind-forged manacles'; critique of institutions.
1842 dramatic monologue; Duke of Ferrara reveals he had wife killed; chilling control.
1854 ballad on Crimean War blunder; 'Theirs not to reason why, theirs but to do and die'; heroic but futile.
Ted Hughes; visceral imagery of soldier mid-charge; questions patriotism; 'King, honour, human dignity, etcetera'.
Simon Armitage on Iraq War PTSD; based on soldier's testimony; 'his blood-shadow stays on the street'.

Paper 1: Poetry and Prose — a core area of GCSE English Literature.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 1: Poetry and Prose brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 1: Poetry and Prose.
